clue.text: Our centenarian, when 28, might say: 'He and I rule Mr Jones when panicking!'

definitions.note: the actor was born in April 1912, so the puzzle marks his hundredth birthday

indicators.note: panicking letters are thrown into confusion, a nod to Corporal Jones's cry of 'Don't panic!'

explanation.surface: Sergeant Wilson, the role at 28 across, gently claims command over the flustered Corporal Jones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when 28, might say' sets the scene: 28 across is Sergeant Wilson, the part this actor played in the BBC sitcom Dad's Army, alongside the excitable Corporal Jones.
explanation.definitionFit: The actor was born in 1912, so in 2012 he was the puzzle's honoured centenary figure.

clue.text: Conclusion's drawn from tiresome gastroscopy

indicators.note: drawn from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A medical report: the end of a tedious stomach examination.
explanation.definitionFit: The last letter of the Greek alphabet stands for the end of anything, as in 'alpha and omega'.

clue.text: No tea to brew? Pop in Walker's 'outlet' — it's close by!

indicators.note: pop in tells us to put the next piece inside the scrambled letters
to brew is to stew or mix up, so the letters of 'No tea' are rearranged

parts.note: the outlet, or exit point, of the word Walker is its last letter, R; Walker is the spiv in Dad's Army

explanation.surface: Private Walker, the black-market spiv, can get tea when it's scarce; his outlet is just round the corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brew' rearranges NO TEA, and 'Pop in' puts R, the last letter of Walker, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean in the vicinity of something, a plain synonym pair.

clue.text: Permanently underlying problem

indicators.note: a problem is something knotty or awry, so the letters of the next word are muddled

explanation.surface: A deep-seated issue that never goes away.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasting for ever and doing so in a lasting way are the same idea, an adverb synonym.

clue.text: Acquire a noisy tea-maker

indicators.note: noisy signals that we want a word that sounds like the next piece

parts.note: an urn is a large vessel for making tea

explanation.surface: Buying a loud kettle.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the vessel and the verb sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To get money or reward by work is a synonym of gaining or obtaining.

clue.text: Snug, maybe — like the Home Guard?

definitions.meaning: the word snug read upwards in a down entry is GUNS, which are arms
armed and ready to fight, as Britain's volunteer wartime force was

explanation.surface: Is a cosy room the right description for Britain's wartime defence volunteers?
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: the word Snug written upward in a down light shows guns, that is, it is 'up' in 'arms'. The Home Guard is the volunteer force of Dad's Army.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means armed and ready to resist, which describes a volunteer defence force.

clue.text: Hi sir! Casserole?

parts.note: the answer read as wordplay says: take letters spelling a nationality, then stew (shuffle) them to get these two words

explanation.surface: A greeting to a gentleman while offering him a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, read as an instruction, says stew the nationality's letters, which gives the clue's 'Hi sir'.
explanation.definitionFit: The dish is a mutton, potato and onion stew, a classic slow-cooked casserole.

clue.text: Limitation head placed on free credit following pause

indicators.note: following tells us the scrambled credit comes after the pause
placed on tells us the headland is added at the end

parts.note: a rest is a pause

indicators.note: free means loose, so the letters of credit are set loose and rearranged

parts.note: a ness is a headland, a head jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: A cap is put on interest-free borrowing after a breathing space.
explanation.definitionFit: Being kept within bounds is the condition of limitation, an abstract noun synonym.

clue.text: Pike, perhaps, after slitting head off methodically, is stiffening in the loft

indicators.note: after places the fish pieces behind the rearranged letters
methodically hints at rearranging the remaining letters in a new order
head off removes the first letter of slitting

parts.note: a pike is a fish, and slit fish gives boneless fillets; Pike is also the young private in Dad's Army

explanation.surface: Private Pike is ordered to prepare a fish and goes rigid up in the attic.
explanation.walkthrough: Deleting the first letter of 'slitting' leaves LITTING, which 'methodically' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: They are wedge-shaped strips of timber under roof tiles, a building term for stiffeners in the roof space.

clue.text: Scandinavian ruminant trapped by Eric, feet first

indicators.note: trapped by tells us the animal goes inside the reordered name
feet first means the end of the name Eric is moved to its front

parts.note: an eland is a large African antelope, a cud-chewing animal

explanation.surface: Eric falls feet first and lands on an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feet first' brings the last two letters of the name to its front, giving ICER, before the antelope goes in. 'Scandinavian' is loose: Iceland is Nordic rather than strictly Scandinavian.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Iceland is a Nordic person, loosely grouped with Scandinavians.

clue.text: Climbers compete in central Lake District

indicators.note: in puts the rivalry word inside the central letters
central picks the two middle letters of the twelve-letter phrase Lake District

parts.note: to vie is to compete

explanation.surface: Mountaineers race each other in the heart of England's Lake District.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lake District is a mountainous region of north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: These evergreen plants climb walls and trees, so they are climbing plants.

clue.text: Characteristic gold winning performance from 1ac as Judas?

definitions.note: the actor won a BAFTA for a 1971 Dennis Potter TV play of this name, playing a defector

parts.note: a trait is a characteristic
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: The prize-winning golden role for the actor in a betrayal story.
explanation.walkthrough: John Le Mesurier won a BAFTA for the TV play of this title; Judas is the archetypal betrayer.
explanation.definitionFit: Judas, who betrayed Jesus, is the archetypal betrayer, and it was also the title of the actor's award-winning play.

clue.text: See 21
Mechanics, having sufficient reason, cried out in triumph

parts.note: ground means a basis or justification, as in grounds for complaint
crew is a past tense of crow, to exult loudly

explanation.surface: Engineers who were justified in celebrating loudly.
explanation.definitionFit: Airfield support staff maintain and service aircraft, so they are mechanics.

clue.text: Botham returns with first of lorries as aid for Frazer's undertaking?

definitions.note: Private Frazer is the Scottish undertaker in Dad's Army; coffins need these fasteners

indicators.note: returns says the first name is read backwards

parts.note: Ian Botham is the famous England cricketer

indicators.note: first of takes the opening letter of lorries

explanation.surface: A cricket hero comes back with a truck to help Frazer with his business.
explanation.definitionFit: An undertaker uses these metal fasteners to secure a coffin lid, so they aid the job.

clue.text: On Firework Night, perhaps, roll up to see original guy?

parts.note: Bonfire Night is the fifth of November, so it falls in Nov, the month abbreviated

indicators.note: up in a down clue tells us the list word is read upwards

parts.note: a rota is a roll or list of duties

explanation.surface: Rolling up on Bonfire Night to see the effigy of Guy Fawkes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ROTA into ATOR. Firework Night is 5 November, when Britain burns 'guy' effigies.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who brings in new ideas is a pioneer, a fellow with original thinking.

clue.text: After he'd sold 100, violinmaker's first to cry 'Boring!'

indicators.note: sold means given away, so the letters of he'd leave the number

parts.note: a hundred written out
taken as its letters H, E, D
Amati was a family of Cremonese violin makers

indicators.note: first to takes the opening letter of cry

explanation.surface: A violin dealer, having made a big sale, protests about how dull it all is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sold' takes H, E and D out of HUNDRED, leaving UNDR.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lacking excitement or theatricality is dull, so the exclamation is a synonym of tedious.

clue.text: Large lid obscuring traditional Cajun stew

indicators.note: obscuring muddles what is visible, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A big pot lid hides a Louisiana dish.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Louisiana dish of meat braised in a rich gravy, a Cajun speciality.

clue.text: What do niggards dare make? (6,6) They make ideal ingredient, said 1ac's Fred!

definitions.text: What do niggards dare make? (6,6) They make ideal ingredient, said 1ac's Fred!

parts.words: What do niggards dare make? (6,6) They make ideal ingredient, said 1ac's Fred!
parts.note: the 1970s Homepride advert, voiced by the actor as the cartoon Fred, said graded grains (an anagram of niggards dare) make this ideal baking ingredient

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about misers, answered by an advertising mascot.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging NIGGARDS DARE gives GRADED GRAINS; the Homepride slogan, spoken by John Le Mesurier as the bowler-hatted Fred, was 'Graded grains make ...' this answer.
explanation.definitionFit: More finely milled baking powder is the ideal cooking base the advert promised.

clue.text: Precious cargo of yacht we expropriated

indicators.note: a cargo is carried inside a vessel, so the answer sits inside these words

explanation.surface: Valuable freight seized from a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Affectedly dainty or quaint is the sense of precious in this British adjective.

clue.text: Very ill, one last breath left, artiste finally composed his last words

indicators.note: composed means put together, so the letters are arranged anew
finally takes the closing letter of artiste

explanation.surface: A dying performer, gravely ill, calmly delivers a farewell line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges VERY ILL, ONE LAST BREATH, L and E. The actor of 1 across is said to have uttered this phrase on his deathbed.
explanation.definitionFit: John Le Mesurier reportedly spoke this gentle phrase just before he died, so it is his parting remark.

clue.text: See 21
Alight from railway during delay — Godfrey finally can be excused!

indicators.note: can be excused lets the letter leave, as Private Godfrey often asks to be excused
during places the railway abbreviation inside the delay word

parts.note: to detain is to delay

indicators.note: finally takes the closing letter of Godfrey

explanation.surface: Getting off a train late, Private Godfrey finally gets his request to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: Godfrey is the elderly Dad's Army private forever asking to be excused. 'during' gives DETRYAIN; 'can be excused' removes Y, Godfrey's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To get off a train is to alight from it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Siege mentality's beginning to infiltrate Alabama and Ohio

indicators.note: to infiltrate puts that letter inside the state abbreviations
beginning takes the opening letter of mentality

explanation.surface: A defensive mindset creeps into two American states.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1836 Texan mission fortress fell after a famous siege, so the name stands for one.

clue.text: See 21
Arthur English backs engaging unknown spotted at rear of the platoon?

definitions.text: spotted at rear of the platoon?
definitions.note: a film walk-on actor might be glimpsed at the back of a marching platoon

indicators.note: engaging means holding the next piece inside
backs means the two pieces are read backwards together

parts.note: Art is a short form of the name Arthur
X is the classic algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Arthur English, comic actor, appears at the back of the platoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backs' turns ARTE into ETRA, and 'engaging' puts X inside. Arthur English was a real British comic actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A background film performer without lines would be seen at the back of the ranks.

clue.text: Peers about to reject a means of access to hearing

indicators.note: about means going round the next pieces

parts.note: earls are peers of the realm
to can is to dismiss or reject, as in getting canned

explanation.surface: Members of the House of Lords are about to turn down a route into a court hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: These passages lead sound to the eardrum, so they are the routes into hearing.

clue.text: Fabric worker's dreadfully slow in completing label for Uncle Arthur

definitions.note: Arthur Wilson's rank and surname, the title Pike's 'Uncle Arthur' goes by

parts.note: serge is a twilled fabric
an ant is the classic worker; the 's stands for is

indicators.note: dreadfully suggests the letters are badly jumbled

explanation.surface: A clothing-factory worker is told off for being slow to finish labelling garments.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dad's Army Arthur Wilson is called 'Uncle Arthur' by young Pike.
explanation.definitionFit: The rank and surname form the formal title by which the character known as Uncle Arthur is addressed.
